newsitem.title: FRANCE: French centre-right widens lead in fresh poll.
newsitem.headline: French centre-right widens lead in fresh poll.

text.p: France's governing centre-right has widened its lead over the left two weeks ahead of the first-round ballot in a snap parliamentary election, according to a new poll made public on Saturday.

The IFOP poll for the weekly Le Journal du Dimanche found a growing gap in voter preference between the current majority and the leftist opposition right, and it translated the right's growing strength into a larger share of seats in the parliament were the election to be held today.

It found the combined right with 41 percent to 38.5 percent for the combined left, 13.5 percent for the extreme-right National Front and seven percent for various ecologist candidates in the first round of the May 25-June 1 election.
In a similar poll conducted a week earlier, the combined right had 38 percent to 41 percent for the combined left, 14 percent for the National Front and seven percent for the ecologists.

In terms of seats, the poll gave the combined right between 328 and 358 seats (versus 269-299 a week earlier), the combined left 193 to 227 seats (versus 255-285), the National Front zero to three seats (versus 0-2) and the ecologists none.

The gains capped a week of unease for the centre-right after earlier polls showed the left growing stronger and a growing chorus of majority voices attacking conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe over his lacklustre campaign leadership.

President Jacques Chirac, wading into the campaign for the first time since dissolving parliament nine months ahead of schedule, penned an opinion article at midweek for regional newspapers blaming France's woes on the previous Socialist administration and urging voters to give him "the political stability indispensible for effective action".

Curiously, however, the IFOP poll found that just 40 percent of French adults were pleased with Chirac's role in the campaign compared to 43 percent unhappy with his performance and 17 percent with no opinion.
The IFOP poll relied on interviews with 914 registered voters and was conducted on Friday.
A second opinion poll, meanwhile, said that the shortness of the campaign would give a boost to candidates on the left.

The Ipsos poll for the weekly Marianne said this was because voters had so little time to learn about their local candidates that they were more likely to vote on the basis of their favourite national party in the May 25-June 1 election.

The left will reap the benefit because there is a smaller proportion of incumbents -- whose names are generally better known to voters than are challengers -- on the left in the outgoing National Assembly than the proportion of leftist voters in the population at large, Ipsos pollsters said.
The current centre-right majority, on the other hand, will suffer because it has a higher percentage of incumbents than its support in the population at large.
Ipsos said the combined left would get 43 percent of the vote based on national party preference compared to 39.5 percent if voters cast their ballots on the basis of candidates' names.

Candidates from the current centre-right majority, on the other hand, would garner 35 percent on the basis of national party preference, compared to 38 percent if choices were made on the basis of candidates' names.
The Ipsos poll was based on interviews with 1,591 people aged 18 and over and was conducted last Tuesday and Wednesday.
